title: Stable stmt-cache slots — removing the move-to-back struct swap (rejected)
impact: The per-connection C statement cache keeps its MRU entry at `entries[count - 1]` and promotes a matched entry by swapping whole structs. `resqlite_cached_stmt` embeds exp 106's `read_tables[64]` (512 B) and `dep_columns[64]` (1 KB) arrays, so one entry is **1,632 bytes** and each promotion moves **4,896 bytes** through three full-struct copies; eviction `memmove`s ~50 KB. Exp 071 and exp 207 both examined this function but measured only the *scan*, on a single repeated SQL — a shape that structurally never pays the swap (the hot entry already sits at the tail, so the promotion branch is skipped). This tested the untouched half: carry LRU ordering in a per-entry recency stamp so slots never move, with in-place min-stamp eviction (identical policy). An isolated C measurement over the real struct layout confirms the mechanism — when the swap fires it costs **~60-65 ns/lookup** (85 vs 21 ns at cache=8, 144 vs 89 at cache=32), and single-SQL controls are flat, proving the branch is inert there. But end-to-end it is invisible: across two order-flipped passes of `stmt_cache_interleaved.dart` no lane reproduces a same-sign win, and the *control* lanes — where both sides run identical code because no swap is reachable — swing +24% / +27% / +103% / +42%. ~65 ns against a ~7-10 us `selectBytes()` round trip is **~0.7% of per-call wall**, an order of magnitude below the harness floor. **Rejected** on exp 071's own methodology (sound, zero-risk, unmeasurable); runtime reverted, prototype at `archive/exp-248`. With scan order (071), scan short-circuit (207), and now promotion cost (248) all measured and immaterial, `stmt_cache_lookup_entry` is closed. Reopen only if the round-trip floor drops ~10x, or a workload appears doing many cache lookups without a round trip per lookup.
